explanation: In the mid-eighteenth century, Carolus Linnaeus developed the system of binomial nomenclature, a standardized way to name species. Under this system, each organism is given a two-part scientific name: the first word is the Genus name (which is capitalized and can be used alone to refer to a group of closely related species), and the second word is the specific epithet (which is lowercase and refers to one specific species within that genus). A species must always be referred to by its full binomial name (Genus species).

questions.q: In binomial nomenclature, what do the first and second words of a scientific name represent?
questions.exp: In the binomial system, the first word is the genus name and the second word is the specific epithet.

questions.q: How must a single species be formally referred to under Linnaeus's binomial system?
opts: By the full binomial name (Genus species)
questions.exp: A species must be referred to by its full binomial name, which includes both the capitalized Genus and the lowercase specific epithet.
